title: Scope, Supervision, and Non-Interpretation

sections.learningObjectives:
- Apply scope-of-practice and supervision boundaries when assisting with ECGs and other diagnostic procedures, performing only trained and delegated tasks.
- Refuse to interpret ECG or other diagnostic results, directing all result and diagnosis questions to the licensed provider.
- Recognize clinical concerns such as chest pain, shortness of breath, and other warning signs, and escalate them promptly through the proper chain of command.
- Decline out-of-scope requests respectfully and seek guidance from a supervisor or provider when unsure whether a task is within scope.
- Document procedures and patient statements objectively, without adding interpretation or diagnosis.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of the ECG as a camera that takes a picture of the little electrical sparks your heart makes each time it squeezes. It does not measure pressure or sounds — just the sparks.

### Question 2

An ECG is like a sticker microphone for your heart — it just listens to the heart's electricity through the skin. Nothing goes inside your body and it does not hurt.

### Question 3

Making the picture and understanding what the picture means are two different jobs. The assistant helps take the picture, but only the doctor is trained to explain what it shows.

### Question 4

The assistant is like the person who sets up a camera and presses the button. Deciding what the picture means and what to do about it is the doctor's job.

### Question 5

If a friend asks you what their drawing means, but you are not the artist, you let the artist explain it. The assistant points the patient to the doctor, who explains the heart picture.

### Question 6

Before taking any picture of the heart, the assistant checks that the doctor asked for it. You do not take pictures nobody ordered.

### Question 7

The ECG is like a detective tool that shows whether the heart's electrical system is working in a steady rhythm. It helps the doctor find problems — it does not fix them.

### Question 8

Before taking the picture, the assistant makes sure they have the right person — like checking a name tag twice before handing over a package.

### Question 9

Stickers stick best to clean, dry skin — just like tape does not stick to a greasy table. Clean skin helps the heart's signals come through clearly.

### Question 10

The stickers go on the arms, legs, and chest — like little listening stations spread around the heart to hear its sparks from every direction.

### Question 11

If the picture suddenly goes blank, the assistant is like a spotter who calls for help right away instead of guessing what happened.

### Question 12

The ECG is a team job — a trained helper runs the machine while a doctor is in charge of what it means and what happens next.

### Question 13

The assistant writes down just the facts, like a careful note-taker — what happened and when — and leaves the opinions to the doctor.

### Question 14

Chest pain is like a fire alarm — you do not ignore it or hope it stops. You get help right away.

### Question 15

If someone's chest hurts, they cannot catch their breath, or their arm or jaw hurts too, that is like a big red flag waving — time to get help fast.

### Question 16

When the machine flashes a warning light, the assistant tells the person in charge — like reporting a strange engine light instead of pretending the car is fine.

### Question 17

It is like a patient asking if a test is a pass. The assistant cannot grade the test — only the doctor can say what it means.

### Question 18

The person who grades the test is the one who explains the grade. The doctor reviews the heart picture and explains it to the patient.

### Question 19

A doctor uses many clues — like a detective uses fingerprints, photos, and witnesses — and the ECG is just one clue in the whole case.

### Question 20

If someone hands you a test and says 'grade it for me,' but you are not the teacher, you hand it back and say, 'the teacher will grade this one.'

### Question 21

The assistant is like a photographer who prints the picture and puts it in the album for the expert to look at — they do not decide what the picture shows.

### Question 22

Cleaning the skin is like wiping a window before taking a photo through it — the clearer the window, the clearer the picture.

### Question 23

Only the doctor can say what is wrong with the heart, like only a mechanic can tell you what is wrong with an engine. The assistant points the patient to the expert.

### Question 24

It is like learning to bake with a grown-up nearby — you do the steps, but someone responsible is watching and can step in if you need help.

### Question 25

Following the recipe is how the dish turns out right every time. The office has a recipe for the ECG, and the assistant follows it.

### Question 26

Running the machine and understanding what the machine found are two different jobs — one is for the helper, the other is for the doctor.

### Question 27

If a patient says their chest has been hurting all week, that is important news the doctor needs to hear right away — like telling a coach when a player says they feel injured.

### Question 28

If a photo comes out blurry because the camera moved, you retake the photo — you do not tell people what the blur 'means.'

### Question 29

When a patient asks what a picture means, the assistant says, 'the doctor is the one who reads this picture and will explain it to you.'

### Question 30

If someone suddenly cannot breathe well, that is a 'tell a grown-up right away' moment — the assistant finds the doctor fast instead of guessing.

### Question 31

Even if a friend asks you to grade a test that is not yours to grade, you say no and point to the teacher — the doctor is the one who reads ECGs.

### Question 32

Good notes are like a reporter's notes — just the facts of what happened, with no opinions about what it means.

### Question 33

If someone starts to get wobbly, you help them sit down safely and call for help — you do not leave them or tell them to walk it off.

### Question 34

Saying 'I'm not trained for that' is like a lifeguard saying they will not perform surgery — it keeps people safe, and it is the right thing to do.

### Question 35

If you are not sure whether you are allowed to do something, ask the person in charge first — it is better than guessing wrong.

### Question 36

Instead of guessing to make someone feel better, the assistant connects the patient with the doctor, who can give a real answer.

### Question 37

If you have never learned to use a machine, you say so and ask to be taught — you do not press buttons and hope it works.

### Question 38

If someone in the waiting room looks like they are in serious trouble, you sound the alarm and get help — you do not wait for their turn.

### Question 39

The assistant writes down exactly what the patient said, like a secretary taking dictation, instead of making up what it means.

### Question 40

Comparing old and new pictures to spot changes is the doctor's job — like a coach reviewing game tapes, not the equipment manager.

### Question 41

The assistant can pass along the doctor's note exactly as written, like a mail carrier delivering a sealed letter — without changing what is inside.

### Question 42

The assistant can say 'those lines are the heart's electrical sparks being drawn on paper,' but what they mean for this person is for the doctor to explain.

### Question 43

Some things are just small requests, but chest pain or a racing heart is a big deal that goes straight to the doctor.

### Question 44

Even if a helper can spot an obvious picture, only the doctor has the training and permission to say what it means for the patient's health.

### Question 45

When a patient asks about their family's heart history, the assistant connects them with the doctor, who is the expert at answering 'what does this mean for me?'

### Question 46

If someone is holding their chest and looks unwell, the assistant checks in and tells the doctor — like telling a teacher when a classmate seems hurt.

### Question 47

If the picture is blurry because the person moved, you ask them to hold still and take it again — you do not guess what the blur shows.

### Question 48

If the machine says a wire came unplugged, the assistant plugs it back in and redoes the picture — they do not pretend the picture is complete.

### Question 49

If someone stops responding, you call for emergency help right away — like shouting for a lifeguard — instead of staring at the screen.

### Question 50

If something feels wrong, it is okay to tell the person in charge — like a lookout who says 'I think I saw something,' even if they are not sure.

### Question 51

The assistant can explain the machine in simple words — 'it listens to your heart's electricity' — but leaves the doctor to explain what it found.

### Question 52

When someone has chest pain, the assistant does not hand out medicine — they get the doctor, who is the only one who should decide about medicine.

### Question 53

The assistant can tell the patient, 'this does not hurt — it just uses stickers to listen to your heart,' which helps them relax.

### Question 54

Only the teacher can say a test is a 'pass.' The assistant helps run the test but does not get to stamp 'normal' on it.

### Question 55

If someone's chest hurts really badly and it spreads to their jaw, that is a 'call 911' moment — you get emergency help right now.

### Question 56

The assistant keeps the camera clean and ready, but does not decide what the pictures mean or how to fix what is in them.

### Question 57

Whether the helper may run the machine is decided by the rules of the place and their training — not by what they or the patient feel like.

### Question 58

If someone asks you to deliver a message you are not sure is true, you check first instead of just repeating it.

### Question 59

Even if a teacher keeps asking a student to grade tests, grading is still the teacher's job — and saying something is the right move.

### Question 60

If a sticker falls off, you put it back on before taking the picture — you do not take a picture with a piece missing.

### Question 61

If you see something strange on the screen, you finish the job and show the expert — you do not guess out loud what it is.

### Question 62

If a patient says 'please do not tell about my chest pain,' the assistant kindly explains that the doctor has to know to keep them safe.

### Question 63

The assistant gets the camera and stickers ready before the picture is taken — but does not decide who needs a picture or what it will show.

### Question 64

If a patient's heart feels like it is racing or fluttering, that is news for the doctor — the assistant passes it along right away.

### Question 65

If a patient has chest tightness and feels sick to their stomach, the assistant tells the doctor first — before doing anything routine.

### Question 66

If the doctor has not actually looked at the test yet, the assistant does not tell the patient the result — they wait for the doctor to look first.

### Question 67

Even if it saves time, the helper cannot do the doctor's job of reading the heart pictures — saying 'no, that is your job' is the right thing.

### Question 68

If the screen changes and the patient feels faint, the assistant keeps them safe and yells for help — they do not stop to name what is on the screen.

### Question 69

The helper can fix stickers and ask the patient to hold still, but saying what the heart rhythm means is the doctor's job.

### Question 70

The assistant can say 'I hear you are worried — let's have the doctor look and explain it,' instead of guessing along with the patient.

### Question 71

Chest pain that comes and goes with activity is like a warning light that flickers — you still take the car to the mechanic, you do not ignore it.

### Question 72

When you say 'that is not my job' and tell the boss, you also write down what happened so everyone has a clear note.

### Question 73

When someone is upset and wants an answer you cannot give, you stay kind, listen, and bring the person who can give the answer.

### Question 74

The safe sentence is: 'this machine listens to your heart's electricity, and the doctor will look at it.'

### Question 75

Instead of saying 'you will be fine' or 'I cannot talk to you,' the assistant says kindly, 'the doctor will look and talk with you.'

### Question 76

What the helper is allowed to do is decided by the rulebook and the boss, and the rules can be different in different places — so the helper has to check.

### Question 77

If the coach is not at the game, the helper checks the rules before playing — you do not just start because the equipment is there.

### Question 78

Saying 'I am not trained for that' keeps people safe, like a student not driving the school bus because they do not have a license.

### Question 79

If the doctor writes the answer, the assistant should not sign it with their own name — the note should say who really did it.

### Question 80

If you tell the boss about a danger and the boss brushes it off, you speak up again or tell the next person in charge — you do not just let it go.

### Question 81

When a patient's heart feels fast and the screen looks strange, the helper keeps the patient safe and gets help fast — they do not try to figure it out alone.

### Question 82

The ECG is like a camera that takes a picture of the heart — it does not fix anything. The doctor uses the picture to decide how to help.

### Question 83

If a family member says the patient has been short of breath at home, the assistant tells the doctor — it is useful information, no matter who says it.

### Question 84

If a patient brings in a report from a gadget at home, the assistant hands it to the doctor to read — like passing homework to the teacher instead of grading it.

### Question 85

Even 'just a quick look' to decide if the doctor should look is still grading the test — that is the doctor's job, so the assistant says no politely.
